strengths: Addresses an important and practical bottleneck in language-based 3D scene understanding: the high latency of autoregressive next-token prediction in models like SceneScript.

Well-tailored adaptation of speculative decoding and multi-token prediction to structured geometric languages, specifically introducing an absolute distance tolerance threshold (tau) for continuous/numerical coordinate tokens.
The proposed confidence-guided decoding (CGD) provides an elegant mechanism to perform on-the-fly token verification without waiting for a subsequent verification step.
The parameter-efficient projection block design effectively mitigates parameter inflation from multiple prediction heads, reducing parameter overhead by ~43% compared to standard MTP.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple benchmarks (ASE, Structured3D, SceneCAD) and tasks (layout estimation and 3D object detection), demonstrating solid wall-clock speedups (~5x) with negligible loss in accuracy.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate, as it combines and adapts known paradigms from LLM inference acceleration (multi-token prediction, Medusa-style heads, self-speculative decoding, and confidence-based stopping) to the structured 3D domain.

A notable empirical discrepancy is that Fast SceneScript (SSD) consistently achieves higher acceptance rates (alpha) and lower latency than CGD across almost all benchmarks (e.g., in Table 1, SSD takes 75 ms with alpha=8.97, while CGD takes 89 ms with alpha=7.27), despite CGD being motivated to eliminate verification delay and save compute. The manuscript lacks an in-depth analysis explaining why SSD remains faster and more effective in practice.

Latency measurements in Tables 1-5 report only the language decoder decoding time rather than end-to-end inference time (including 3D point cloud feature extraction via the sparse 3D ResNet encoder). Clarifying end-to-end wall-clock latency would provide a more complete picture of real-world efficiency gains.

strengths: Clear motivation and practical impact: Accelerating structured language models for 3D scene understanding is an important and timely problem, as autoregressive next-token prediction introduces significant latency during inference.

Domain-tailored technical contributions: The adaptation of speculative decoding with distance tolerance (tau) for continuous numerical coordinates and the confidence-guided decoding (CGD) mechanism effectively exploit the structured nature of 3D scene representations.

Parameter-efficient design: Sharing projection blocks and prediction heads across future token positions mitigates the severe parameter overhead typical of multi-token prediction models (~43% parameter reduction compared to standard MTP heads with negligible accuracy loss).

Strong empirical results: Fast SceneScript achieves around 5x speedup across layout estimation and object detection tasks on ASE, Structured3D, and SceneCAD datasets, maintaining or slightly improving accuracy relative to the SceneScript baseline while drastically outperforming naive MTP.
weaknesses: Incremental conceptual novelty: The underlying paradigms (multi-token prediction, self-speculative decoding, and confidence-based early stopping) are adapted from existing LLM inference acceleration works (e.g., Medusa, Blockwise parallel decoding, Draft&Verify), with the main novelty lying in their adaptation to structured 3D coordinate tokens.

Latency vs. throughput trade-offs between SSD and CGD: In several quantitative results (e.g., Table 1 and Table 2), SSD achieves higher average accepted tokens per step (alpha) and lower latency than CGD, despite CGD being motivated by avoiding verification delay. A clearer discussion on the overhead of confidence prediction versus speculative re-drafting would strengthen the analysis.

Evaluation scope: The evaluation is concentrated on SceneScript-based representations on synthetic (ASE, Structured3D) and relatively small real-world datasets (SceneCAD). Demonstrating broader applicability across other multimodal 3D representations or large-scale real-world datasets (e.g., ScanNet) would make the findings more impactful.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical bottleneck: autoregressive structured language models for 3D perception (e.g., SceneScript) suffer from substantial latency due to sequential next-token prediction, which limits real-time application.

Well-motivated adaptations tailored to structured 3D languages: introducing numerical distance tolerance (tau) for spatial coordinate tokens prevents unnecessary speculative rejection, and Confidence-Guided Decoding (CGD) enables effective single-pass on-the-fly verification without requiring speculative verification forward passes.

Parameter-efficient design: the shared projection and head architecture mitigates parameter bloat typically associated with multi-token prediction heads, adding only ~7.5% extra parameters while outperforming naive separate-head MTP baselines.

Strong and consistent empirical performance: achieves ~5x wall-clock speedup across layout estimation and object detection on multiple synthetic and real-world datasets (ASE, Structured3D, SceneCAD) while preserving or slightly improving F1 accuracy.

Thorough ablation studies: clear evaluations validate the choice of tolerance threshold tau, confidence threshold epsilon, head sharing, supervision targets for the confidence head, and head scaling up to n=16.
weaknesses: The core ideas of multi-token prediction and self-speculative decoding are largely adapted from recent NLP literature (e.g., Medusa, Gloeckle et al., Draft&Verify); while the numerical distance relaxation and confidence head are sensible domain-specific adaptations, the methodological novelty is somewhat incremental.

The evaluation is primarily restricted to small specialized decoders (~14M parameters). It remains unclear whether the observed latency speedups and verification dynamics hold similarly for large-scale multimodal models (e.g., 7B backbones such as SpatialLM) where memory bandwidth and batching profiles differ substantially.

Object detection annotations on the ASE dataset are synthetically generated using a pre-trained detector (TR3D) rather than human-verified 3D bounding boxes, which introduces some potential evaluation noise, though this is partially mitigated by validation on SceneCAD.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical bottleneck in language-based 3D scene perception: autoregressive next-token prediction (NTP) causes significant latency during sequential generation of structured representations.

The adaptation of multi-token prediction and speculative decoding to structured perception tokens is well-tailored, specifically introducing a distance tolerance metric for numerical layout coordinates/dimensions and Confidence-Guided Decoding (CGD) for on-the-fly filtering without redundant verification passes.

The parameter-efficient head-sharing design with an intermediate projection block effectively addresses the parameter expansion typical of multi-head MTP models, saving over 40% parameters while preserving task performance.

Strong empirical efficiency gains across two standard benchmarks (ASE and Structured3D), achieving approximately 5x speedup with comparable or marginally superior F1-scores compared to autoregressive SceneScript baselines.
weaknesses: Task breadth is limited: although SceneScript originally handles multiple 3D perception tasks (including 3D bounding box detection and CAD part reconstruction), the evaluation is restricted to 3D scene layout estimation (wall, window, door). Demonstrating generalization across other structured 3D output formats would substantially strengthen the claims.

The conceptual novelty is moderate: multi-token prediction, speculative decoding, and confidence-based early stopping are established techniques in the general LLM literature (e.g., Medusa, Draft & Verify); the primary contribution lies in adapting and tuning these techniques to structured perception tokens.

Inference profiling lacks deeper systems-level analysis: decoding latency is reported only on a single desktop GPU (RTX 2080 Ti). Further analysis covering memory bandwidth, KV-cache behavior, and varying batch sizes would give a clearer picture of deployment scalability.

strengths: Substantial and practical inference speedup: Fast SceneScript accelerates autoregressive generation by ~5.1x to 5.6x on ASE and Structured3D while maintaining or slightly improving layout estimation F1 scores, addressing a critical bottleneck in structured 3D perception models.

Well-motivated domain-specific adaptations: Extending self-speculative decoding with a relaxed tolerance margin for continuous/numerical tokens (e.g., coordinates and dimensions) is well-suited to structured 3D representations.

Comprehensive decoding analysis: The paper provides a thorough exploration of both speculative verification (SSD) and on-the-fly confidence-guided decoding (CGD), comparing them against standard probability-based thresholds (SoftmaxThre, ProductThre).

Parameter efficiency: The shared head architecture with lightweight projection blocks effectively controls the parameter footprint of multi-token prediction (adding only ~7.5% parameters compared to >60-80% in standard MTP).
weaknesses: Limited task breadth compared to the original SceneScript: While SceneScript was introduced as a multi-task generalist (covering scene layout estimation, 3D bounding box detection, and coarse object part reconstruction), this work restricts its evaluation solely to 3D scene layout estimation.

Conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental: The core mechanisms (multi-token prediction heads, speculative verification, confidence/auxiliary heads) are largely adaptations of existing LLM acceleration frameworks (e.g., Medusa, Blockwise parallel decoding, Draft & Verify) applied to the 3D domain.

Lack of discussion on KV-cache management and memory overhead: The paper discusses latency and parameter counts, but does not detail how KV-caching is handled during the drafting and verification phases in SSD vs. CGD, or its impact on peak GPU memory usage during batched inference.

strengths: Practical and timely problem formulation: Autoregressive structured language models for 3D perception (such as SceneScript) suffer from significant latency due to sequential token generation; accelerating inference without sacrificing layout precision is of high practical value.

Effective domain-specific adaptations: Adapting speculative decoding to structured geometric language by introducing an L1 distance tolerance threshold (tau) for continuous/numerical tokens is intuitive and well-suited for 3D perception outputs.

Strong empirical speedup with minimal degradation: The proposed Fast SceneScript achieves approximately 5.09x to 5.57x speedup compared to standard SceneScript on ASE and Structured3D, while maintaining comparable F1-scores, effectively overcoming the severe quality degradation of naive multi-token prediction (MTP).
Parameter-efficient design: By sharing prediction heads and employing lightweight projection blocks, the model saves ~43% to 48% parameter overhead compared to standard multi-head MTP configurations.

Comprehensive ablations: The paper provides informative ablations analyzing the distance threshold tau, comparison between self-speculative decoding (SSD) and confidence-guided decoding (CGD), as well as comparisons against existing probability-thresholding baselines.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual and methodological novelty: The core components—multi-token prediction (MTP), self-speculative decoding (SSD), and parallel confidence heads—are largely direct adaptations of established techniques from NLP and LLM acceleration literature (e.g., Gloeckle et al., Medusa, Draft & Verify). The technical novelty is primarily incremental engineering for structured 3D layout strings.

Narrow evaluation scope across 3D perception tasks: SceneScript was introduced as a generalist structured language model capable of 3D layout estimation, 3D object detection, and coarse CAD part reconstruction. However, this paper exclusively evaluates layout estimation (walls, windows, doors). Demonstrating the applicability of Fast SceneScript to 3D bounding box prediction or CAD generation would significantly strengthen the claims of general applicability.

Lack of latency breakdown across pipeline stages: Inference latency is reported in absolute milliseconds for the decoding stage, but the paper does not clearly present the end-to-end breakdown between the 3D point cloud feature extraction (sparse 3D ResNet) and the language decoder forward passes under different batch sizes.

Sensitivity and overhead analysis of hyperparameters: In CGD, the performance relies on the confidence threshold epsilon and the training loss weights. A more detailed sensitivity analysis regarding how epsilon trades off acceptance rate (alpha) against layout precision across diverse scene complexities is lacking in the main text.
